title: Generative AI vs predictive AI: which does your workflow need?
description: Which of your workflows need predictive AI, generative AI, both or neither: study results, dated prices, current rules and who signs off.
job: deciding which kind of AI fits a workflow
verdict: Use predictive AI if the job is a number from your own records, such as demand, cash or default risk[^1][^2].
Use generative AI if the job is reading or writing: drafts, summaries, fields pulled from documents. A person checks it[^1][^3].
Use both if the facts sit in documents but the decision is a score: generative extracts, predictive scores[^4][^5].
Use neither if a spreadsheet forecast or a written rule already works. Make any AI beat it first[^6][^7].
Either way, people decide: lenders must give specific denial reasons, and chatbots state wrong answers with confidence[^8][^9].

onPage.text: Three builds: a scorecard, a forecast, a document check
Who decides, who checks and who signs off
Ten common workflows, mapped to the AI each needs
Mistakes teams make when choosing, and the fix for each
Straight answers to the questions buyers ask

summary: Predictive AI turns your past records into a number, such as demand or default risk, while generative AI writes new content, such as drafts.[^10][^11][^9][^1] The output decides it: a tested number, or words a person checks.[^1][^12]

tables.title: How do predictive and generative AI differ in practice?
tables.intro: Generative AI here means large language models (LLMs), the engines behind ChatGPT and similar chatbots[^9]. SR 26-2 is the bank regulators' model risk guidance; it replaced SR 11-7 on 17 Apr 2026[^13][^14][^15]. Reg B is the US rule on credit decisions and the reasons for each denial[^8].

rows.name: What goes in
cells: Rows and columns from your own records: past sales, loan files, payment history[^10][^12]
A prompt plus text, documents or images. The model was trained beforehand on huge public data[^9][^11]

rows.name: What comes out
cells: A number, score or probability: a forecast, a default risk, a fraud flag[^10][^11]
New content: a draft, a summary, an answer or fields pulled from a document[^9][^16]

rows.name: Data you supply
cells: Your own labelled history, often a few GB or less (AWS's description)[^17][^11]
A few examples and your documents at run time. The model itself was trained on terabytes (AWS's description)[^17]

rows.name: How you test it
cells: Hide past months or loans the model never saw, then compare its predictions with what happened[^13][^18]
Check outputs against a verified answer key: field accuracy for extraction, error rate on a question set[^3][^19]

rows.name: Typical jobs
cells: Demand and cash forecasts, credit scores, churn risk, fraud flags[^1][^11][^20]
Drafting, summarising, questions about documents, data extraction, chat[^1][^16]

rows.name: How you pay
cells: Build once, then score cheaply. No-code tools bill by use, such as $1.90 per session-hour on SageMaker Canvas, read 26 Nov 2026[^21]
Per token, every time it runs: about $2 in and $10 out per million tokens on mid-tier models[^22][^23]. Third-party tracker prices, read 26 Nov 2026

rows.name: Can it explain itself?
cells: Simple and additive models give exact reasons for each decision[^24][^25]
Usually not: IBM says most generative models lack explainability (IBM's view)[^11]. Confident wrong answers are a named risk[^9]

rows.name: How it fails
cells: Drift: accuracy decays as the world moves away from the training data[^10][^26]
Confabulation: fluent, confident and wrong[^9][^27][^19]

rows.name: US rules that apply
cells: Reg B reasons for credit denials[^8]. SR 26-2 for bank models; the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) bulletin for insurers[^13][^10]
Reg B still applies to any credit decision[^8]. SR 26-2 leaves generative AI out of scope, and you still own what your chatbot says[^13][^28]

tables.title: What happened when the two went head to head?
tables.intro: Published studies, with sample sizes; XGBoost and LightGBM are common boosted-tree models. AUC scores how well a model ranks risk, from 0.5 (a coin flip) to 1 (perfect)[^29][^2]. On numbers from records, trained models won; on documents, LLMs did the reading[^30][^4][^3].

rows.name: Ferro Pérez et al. 2026, cooperative lending, Colombia (university paper)
cells: 12,861 loans, 17.3% default rate[^2]
Tuned ML scored AUC about 0.96; gpt-4o-mini 0.67-0.74[^2]. Trained models overtook the LLM after about 40-80 labelled loans[^2]

rows.name: Huertas (Amazon), FedCSIS 2024
cells: 4 public datasets, incl. FICO home-equity loans[^29]
FICO AUC: GPT-4 0.68, XGBoost 0.72, plain logistic regression 0.72[^29]. The LLM won only with 8 or fewer examples[^29]

rows.name: Drinkall et al., FinNLP 2025
cells: Corporate credit ratings[^4]
XGBoost on the numbers: 52.8% accuracy; GPT-4o: 31.4%[^4]. XGBoost on the numbers plus GPT-4o reading the text: 69.9%[^4]

rows.name: Grinsztajn et al., NeurIPS 2022
cells: 45 tabular datasets[^30]
Tree-based models stayed state of the art on medium-sized data, about 10,000 rows[^30]

rows.name: M5 forecasting competition, IJF 2022
cells: 42,840 Walmart sales series[^18]
Winner beat the best statistical benchmark by 22.4%; the boosted-tree method LightGBM dominated[^18]

rows.name: Tan et al., NeurIPS 2024
cells: 3 LLM forecasting methods, 13 datasets[^31]
Removing the LLM did not hurt accuracy and often helped, at far less compute[^31]

rows.name: Ansari et al., Chronos (Amazon), TMLR 2024
cells: 42 datasets[^32]
A purpose-built pretrained forecasting model did well with no training on the data. It is a forecasting tool, not a chatbot[^32]

rows.name: Berghaus et al. (Fraunhofer), 2025
cells: 8 LLMs, 3 invoice and receipt datasets[^3]
Best field accuracy: 96.5% clean invoices, 92.7% scanned invoices, 87.5% receipts[^3]. Bank-number fields were weakest[^3]

rows.name: Magesh et al. (Stanford), JELS 2025
cells: 202 legal research questions[^19]
Purpose-built legal AI tools gave false answers 17-33% of the time; GPT-4 43%[^19]

tables.note: Newer tabular foundation models such as TabPFN now rival boosted trees in a third-party benchmark[^33]. The line is blurring, but a chatbot prompt is still not a forecasting model[^31][^32].

recipes.name: 1. Lending or underwriting team: a credit scorecard (predictive)
recipes.when: A lender or insurer with 2+ years of decided files and known outcomes. Past about 40-80 labelled loans, trained models beat an LLM on this job[^2][^29].
flow: Head of credit: define the outcome, such as 90+ days past due within 24 months[^25]
Credit analyst: pull past applications and outcomes, and set aside the newest ones untouched[^13]
Credit analyst: fit a logistic regression and an explainable boosted model, then compare them on the set-aside loans[^29][^24]
Independent reviewer: challenge the inputs, the logic and the result on the set-aside loans[^13]
Credit officer: run it in shadow on one loan product, beside today's decisions, before it decides anything
Underwriter: decide every decline and borderline case, and give the top reasons the model used[^8]
Model owner: check accuracy monthly and re-fit when the applicant mix shifts[^10][^26]
recipes.cost: Open-source tools are free[^36]; no-code SageMaker Canvas is $1.90 per session-hour after a free tier, read 26 Nov 2026[^21]. Twenty build hours past the free tier is $38 (our arithmetic).

recipes.name: 2. FP&A or planning team: a demand or cash forecast (predictive first)
recipes.when: A finance or planning team with 2-3 years of weekly or monthly history in a spreadsheet. Predictive methods make the number; generative AI only drafts the commentary[^1][^18].
flow: FP&A analyst: build an Excel Forecast Sheet, which shows a 95% band and error stats[^6]
FP&A analyst: hide the last 6-12 months, forecast them, and record the error as the bar to beat[^18][^7]
FP&A analyst: if many items or drivers matter, test a boosted-tree model and keep it only if it beats the bar[^18]
FP&A lead: own the number and log every manual override
Generative AI: draft the variance commentary from the approved numbers[^1]
FP&A analyst: check every figure in the draft before it goes out[^9]
recipes.cost: Excel's forecast tools come with desktop Microsoft 365[^34]. Commentary for 20 reports a month is about $0.40 at third-party tracker prices read 26 Nov 2026 (our arithmetic)[^22][^23].

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy team: generative reads, predictive scores (both)
recipes.when: Small-business lending, commercial insurance or payables teams whose facts sit in bank statements, invoices or applications. In one study, a boosted model plus LLM-read text lifted credit-rating accuracy from 52.8% to 69.9%[^4][^5].
flow: Ops lead: list the 10-15 fields the decision needs
Generative AI: pull those fields from each document[^3]
Ops reviewer: check amounts, bank numbers and low-confidence fields, where models err most[^3]
Predictive model: score the case from the checked fields plus history[^4][^5]
Underwriter: decide, and sign off the reasons[^8]
recipes.cost: Extraction for 1,000 documents a month is about $11 on a mid-tier model, or $0.55 on a small one (our arithmetic)[^22][^23]. Prices are third-party, read 26 Nov 2026; your reviewers' time is the bigger cost.

humanRole: Underwriter or credit officer: makes every decline call and signs its reasons; the model only ranks. Reg B reasons must be specific and match the factors actually scored[^8].

Independent reviewer, not the builder: challenges each model's inputs, logic and results on held-back cases before use. SR 26-2 keeps this 'effective challenge' for bank models, vendor models included[^13][^14].
Model owner: watches accuracy and calls the re-fit. The NAIC bulletin asks insurers to assess drift, and FICO scores lost predictive power from 2003 to 2006[^10][^26].
A named person approves any generated text before a customer sees it. A tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's wrong fare advice[^28][^9].

ownData.title: Which kind of AI does each common workflow need?
ownData.intro: Zavient desk mapping, 26 Nov 2026: ten workflows a 40-500 person lender, insurer or finance team commonly owns. We placed each against Gartner's use-case families, then checked it against the studies above[^1][^30][^18]. Six are prediction jobs, three are reading or writing jobs, and one needs both.
rows: Credit scoring for loan applicants
Predictive[^8][^29][^2]
2+ years of decided applications with repayment outcomes
AUC on loans it never saw; predicted default rates match actual ones
Demand forecast (stock, staffing)
Predictive, or a spreadsheet forecast[^1][^18][^31][^6]
2-3 years of weekly or monthly history, plus promotions and price
Forecast hidden past months; beat the error of an Excel forecast
13-week cash forecast
Predictive, or a spreadsheet forecast[^1][^7][^6]
Receipts and payments history, receivables and payables ageing
Forecast hidden past weeks; track the error weekly against actuals
Collections prioritisation
Predictive[^10][^30][^20]
Payment history and contact outcomes per account
On held-back months, do top-ranked accounts pay, or fall further behind, more often?
Fraud or anomaly flags
Predictive; Gartner rates generative only 'somewhat useful'[^1][^36]
Labelled past fraud and normal transactions
Share of flags that were real, and share of fraud caught, on a held-back month
Churn or lapse risk
Predictive[^10][^36]
Tenure, usage, service and billing history
Does the retention team keep more customers with the list than without?
Invoice and statement field extraction
Generative[^3]
Sample documents and an answer key of correct fields
Field accuracy on 100+ checked documents; extra checks on bank numbers and totals
Claims or application triage from notes
Both: generative reads, predictive scores[^4][^5][^10]
Free-text notes plus outcomes for past cases
Field accuracy on a checked sample, then a score check on held-back past cases
Customer email and letter drafting
Generative; a person approves[^9][^28][^1]
Approved templates, policy text, tone examples
Reviewer error rate on sample drafts; no wrong policy statements
Contract or policy questions
Generative, answering from your own documents; a person verifies[^27][^19][^1]
The contracts and policies themselves
An answer key of 50+ questions; count wrong or unsupported answers
ownData.note: Method: desk mapping, not a benchmark we ran, so sample sizes are the cited studies', not ours. All sources read 26 Nov 2026; your own data can change a placement. Re-check by 26 May 2027.

example.input: A 120-person small-business lender. An analyst reads three months of bank statements per application and keys 12 fields into a spreadsheet. Someone suggests asking a chatbot whether to approve, though on 12,861 real loans a chatbot model ranked risk far worse than trained ML[^2].
example.output: Generative AI pulls the 12 fields, and an ops reviewer checks amounts and account numbers[^3]. A boosted model trained on 4,000 past loans gives a default probability, tested on 1,000 more held back[^2][^18]. The underwriter decides and sends the top reasons the model actually used[^8].

watchOuts: Asking a chatbot for the forecast number: Gartner rates generative AI 'hardly useful' for forecasting[^1][^37]. Use a forecasting method and test it on hidden past months; removing the LLM from LLM forecasters often improved accuracy[^31].
Testing once, or never: score every model on months or loans it never saw before go-live, as the M5 and M4 contests did[^18][^7]. Then re-check monthly, because models decay as data shifts[^13][^26].

Treating a chatbot's odds as a risk number: in one lending study it predicted 28-38% default against an actual 17%[^2]. For anything that sets price, limit or reserve, use a predictive model whose predicted rates match real ones[^2][^24].

A black box where reasons are required: Reg B still demands specific reasons tied to the factors actually scored[^8]. The CFPB withdrew its two AI-related adverse-action circulars in May 2025, but the rule itself stands[^38][^39].

Publishing generated answers unchecked: Air Canada was held liable for its chatbot's advice[^28]. Even purpose-built legal AI tools gave false answers 17-33% of the time, so a named person approves outbound text[^19].

Citing SR 11-7 as current: SR 26-2 replaced it on 17 Apr 2026 and leaves generative AI out of scope[^13][^14][^15]. It targets banks over $30B in assets, but it is the clearest public guide to good model practice for any lender[^13][^15].

faq.q: Is ChatGPT generative AI or predictive AI?
faq.a: Generative: it predicts the next word inside, but what it gives you is new content, not a tested forecast or score[^9][^11].

faq.q: Can generative AI do forecasting or predictive analytics?
faq.a: Not well as a chatbot: Gartner rates it 'hardly useful' for forecasting, and removing the LLM from three forecasting methods did not hurt accuracy[^1][^31]. Purpose-built time-series models are a different tool, and some do well[^32].

Yes, for the rules: the NAIC bulletin calls it a predictive model, and SR 26-2 counts any method producing quantitative estimates as a model[^10][^13]. On FICO credit data, a plain logistic regression matched a boosted-tree model (XGBoost) at 0.72 AUC[^29].

faq.q: Is generative AI replacing predictive AI?
faq.a: No: Gartner says nongenerative machine learning is superior for prediction, and that focusing only on generative AI is 'a guarantee to fail'[^1]. The best credit-rating result in one study combined both[^4].

faq.q: Which type of AI is better for business?
faq.a: Neither wins everywhere; the output decides. Numbers from your own records point to predictive AI, and words and documents point to generative AI[^1][^12].

faq.q: What is the difference between agentic, generative and predictive AI?
faq.a: Predictive AI scores outcomes from past records, while generative AI writes content and agentic AI plans and acts with tools.[^11][^40][^20] One agent flow can call a predictive score and a generative model, per IBM's and SAP's explainers.[^40][^20] Our agentic AI vs generative AI comparison covers the third kind.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the job is standard, such as document extraction, drafting or a forecast inside your planning tool, and you have no data team[^41]. In a Menlo Ventures survey of US enterprise decision-makers, 76% of AI use cases were bought in 2025, up from 53% in 2024[^41]. MIT NANDA found bought tools succeeded about 67% of the time, twice the rate of internal builds, though both studies cover generative AI only[^42][^43].
buyVsBuild.build: Build, or set up a no-code tool on your own data, when your history is the edge, such as a credit or claims score[^17][^21]. No-code options start at $1.90 per session-hour, read 26 Nov 2026[^21]. Either way, validate a vendor's model as you would your own[^13].

pickElse: A spreadsheet forecast already works: Excel's Forecast Sheet gives a forecast, a 95% band and error stats[^34][^6]. In the M4 contest, simple statistical combinations ranked among the most accurate methods[^7].
The decision is a fixed policy, such as declining above a set debt-to-income ratio: write the rule into your loan system. SR 26-2 doesn't count deterministic rules as models[^13].
A plain scorecard is enough: logistic regression matched a boosted-tree model on FICO credit data, and its reasons are easy to explain[^29][^25].
Too little history: below about 40-80 decided loans, trained models had too little to learn from in one lending study[^2]. Keep deciding by policy and log clean outcomes until you have enough[^29].

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing (18 Aug 2025)
sources.what: Fortune's write-up of MIT NANDA's The GenAI Divide report. Headline: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing; about 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration, while the vast majority stall with little to no measurable P&L impact. Purchasing AI tools from specialized vendors and building partnerships succeed about 67% of the time. Its comparison for internal builds misstates the report, where internal builds reach deployment about a third of the time: cite this write-up for the 67% and its headline figures only; MIT's report carries the internal-build rate and the "twice" comparison. Read 28 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Not sure your forecast or scorecard needs generative AI?
offer.body: If the output is a number, such as a forecast or score, you need predictive AI; generative AI only helps with the text around it. In a free 30-minute call, we check one workflow you own and name the test to run before you spend.

reviews.notes: Wants to know which workflow goes to which kind of AI and how to prove it works before go-live. The workflow map answers both: a main fit and a test for each of ten jobs. The 'On this page' list follows page order. Recipe 2's name ran long on a phone; shortened to 'FP&A or planning team: a demand or cash forecast (predictive first)'. No sourced time-to-deploy figure exists in the research, so none is given.

Reads on a phone between meetings. Jargon cut: 'backtest', 'holdout', 'roll' and 'calibrated' became plain descriptions (forecast hidden past months, set-aside loans, fall further behind, predicted rates match real ones). Map cells shortened so the 4-column table fits a phone. XGBoost and LightGBM are now explained once as boosted-tree models; the FAQ and pick-neither lines say 'boosted-tree model'.

Asks whether one unit can try it first and what it really costs. Added a step to the scorecard build: run it in shadow on one loan product beside today's decisions before it decides anything. The document recipe's token cost (about $11 a month) looked too cheap to trust; it now says reviewers' time is the bigger cost. Token prices stay labelled third-party with the date read.

Head of lending or underwriting asks what the examiner will ask. The SR 11-7 watch-out now says SR 26-2 targets banks over $30B but is the clearest public guide for any lender, so a smaller lender doesn't over-read it. CFPB circulars are shown as withdrawn in May 2025, with Reg B's specific-reasons duty still in force. The Colombian lending study is labelled a university paper on one market, in the table and the key numbers.

Steve gets the answer in 10 seconds: the title is his question and the bottom line is five 'use X if' bullets. Every tool shows a dated price or says it is a third-party price. His return worry is answered by testing before spending: each mapped workflow names the test to pass, and 'use neither' sets a spreadsheet as the bar. A survey stat on AI profit impact was tried and cut, because it isn't used elsewhere on the page. The research has no source on data security for this choice and no case from a firm his size, so neither is claimed; the example is marked illustrative.

answers.recipes: A lending team scoring loans fits predictive AI, a planning team forecasting cash fits predictive first, and a document-heavy team fits both: generative reads, predictive scores[^1][^4].
answers.human-role: Your team keeps every decision: an underwriter signs each decline, an independent reviewer challenges each model, a model owner watches accuracy, and a named person approves generated text[^8][^13].
answers.example: At a 120-person small-business lender, generative AI pulls 12 fields from bank statements, a predictive model scores default risk, and the underwriter decides[^3][^2][^8].
answers.what-goes-wrong: Teams go wrong by asking a chatbot for a number a tested model should make, skipping tests on unseen data, and publishing generated text unchecked[^1][^18][^28].
answers.something-else: Pick neither when a spreadsheet forecast already works, the decision is a fixed policy rule, a plain scorecard is enough, or you have too little history[^6][^13][^29][^2].
answers.table-1: Predictive AI turns your own records into a tested number, while generative AI turns a prompt and documents into new text that a person checks[^10][^9].
answers.table-2: On numbers from records, trained predictive models beat the chatbots, while on documents the LLMs did the reading well[^30][^4][^3].
answers.table-3: The predictive tools are free or bundled, except SageMaker Canvas at $1.90 a session-hour, while mid-tier LLM APIs cost about $2 in and $10 out per million tokens[^34][^35][^21][^22].
answers.own-data: Of ten common workflows, six need predictive AI, three need generative AI, and one, claims or application triage, needs both[^1][^4].
